Leading with Care

Thank your nanny. Then help change her industry.

by Naaz Nichols, CXOPublished on: September 24, 20265 min read
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:35
Instaread

This week, I called two nannies and read them the reviews their families wrote about them, word for word. It was emotional for all. But this isn’t really a story about a nice phone call — it’s about why families need nannies more than they ever have, why most of that work still happens off the books, and what it would actually take to change that. National Nanny Recognition Week wraps up this weekend. I don’t want it to end with a thank-you and nothing else.

Why we need nannies more than ever

Our 2026 Cost of Care Report surveyed 3,000 parents earlier this year, and the picture it paints is stark. 90% say they’ve lost sleep over child care logistics. 89% feel burnt out. 88% say they’re sacrificing other goals in life just to keep it all running. 

At the same time, the people who do this work for a living are harder to find than ever. Child care employment collapsed by more than 30% during the pandemic and still hasn’t fully recovered, and it’s not a mystery why: when a field doesn’t offer competitive pay or basic protections, people leave it for jobs that do.

So it’s not that parents are failing to manage. It’s that a shrinking, undersupported workforce is being asked to hold up a system too many families depend on, and the nannies still doing this work, and doing it well, are doing it despite an industry that hasn’t made it easy to stay. The early mornings, the school pickups, the sick days no one saw coming, the version of “help” that actually holds a household together — that’s the job, carried by fewer people than it should be.

Three of the people doing that work

Emmys has been described as a “lifesaver” and “blessing” by parents of babies and toddlers in her care; they talk about their children absolutely loving her, which is praise we never grow tired of hearing. Megan spent more than two years with a family, walking in as a stranger to a 3-month-old and a 3-year-old, and walking out as someone who celebrated their milestones like her own. Sierra has the kind of range that lets her show up for a newborn one week and an 8-year-old the next, and every family she’s worked with says the same thing: she just handles it.

They’re the reason a lot of families are still standing, and this week, we got to celebrate that with all three of them, live, with the family’s own words.

Why gratitude isn’t nearly enough

For as long as I can remember, this industry has run on a quiet assumption that caregiving is something you do out of love, not something you do as a career. By some estimates, the vast majority of nannies in the U.S. are still paid off the books, which means most of the people doing this work may not have a single hour of it counted toward Social Security, unemployment protection, or a documented income history if they ever needed one.

I understand why families default to that. I also understand why some nannies ask for it too — when money is already tight, a bigger number in cash can feel a lot more real than a smaller one on paper with taxes withheld, even when the paper version is protecting you. And then there’s the search itself: finding someone you trust completely, who fits your family, who your kids actually love, is hard. By the time a family finds that person, and cash is the one condition standing between them and saying yes, most parents will take the deal. I don’t think that makes anyone wrong. I think it makes the whole system fragile — resting on individual families and individual nannies to sort out something that should never have been left to them alone.

Here’s what gets left on the table when we default to cash: a documented income history that can get you approved for an apartment or a car loan. Social Security and Medicare credits. Unemployment insurance and workers’ comp if something goes wrong. In a lot of states, real PTO. None of that exists in a cash arrangement. All of it exists the second a family decides this is a job, not a casual side hustle.

A call to do both

Here’s what I implore all families to do.

Say thank you. Today, not “eventually.” Tell your nanny, specifically, what you’ve noticed — the thing only she would know to do, the way she handles a bad morning, the fact that your kid lights up when she walks in. That costs nothing and takes five minutes, and it still matters more than you’d think.

But don’t stop there. If any of this sounds like your own nanny, ask yourself honestly how she’s being paid, and what it would actually take to change that. It’s rarely as complicated or as expensive as it sounds — Care.com’s HomePay team walks families through exactly this, from the first tax form to the first paycheck. Talk to other parents about this, too, because the societal norm needs to change. To elevate nannying as a profession and ensure caregivers get the benefits they deserve, all of us need to decide, together, that this is a real job with real protections.

Happy National Nanny Recognition Week. To Emmys, Megan, Sierra — and everyone doing this work quietly, every single day — we see you. Let’s make sure the industry does, too.
